text:
Elbaz v. Elbaz

29 O.R. (2d) 207

114 D.L.R. (3d) 116

ONTARIO

HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE

PENNELL, J.

11TH JULY 1980.

Family law -- Divorce -- Cruelty -- Wife obtaining abortion without knowledge or consent of husband -- Whether conduct amounting to cruelty -- Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. D-8, s. 3(d).
Where the wife's procurement of an abortion without her husband's knowledge or consent has some emotional impact upon the husband, but does not have a significant effect on his physical or mental health, and does not, taken alone or in conjunction with other relevant circumstances, render intolerable continued cohabitation, such conduct does not constitute cruelty within the meaning of s. 3(d) of the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. D-8.
Family law -- Custody -- Access -- Custody awarded to parent of orthodox Jewish faith -- Children raised in orthodox faith -- Other parent proposing week-end activities inconsistent with religion -- Appropriate terms for access.
Where custody is granted in favour of a parent who observes the orthodox Jewish religion, access to the other parent who proposes week-end activities inconsistent with such religion may still be ordered. However, when exercising her right to access, the other parent should ensure that the children, so far as is reasonably possible, observe the practices of the religion in which they are to be raised.
PETITION for divorce and custody.

[Knoll v. Knoll,
1970 CanLII 469 (ON CA)
, [1970] 2 O.R. 169, 10 D.L.R. (3d) 199, 1 R.F.L. 141; Lauder v. Lauder, [1949] P. 277, refd to]

[Re K (Minors),
[1977] 2 W.L.R. 33
, refd to]

Leonard Levencrown, for petitioner.
Craig Callan-Jones, for respondent.

PENNELL, J.:-- In these proceedings, the petitioner husband
presented a petition for divorce on the ground of cruelty and
prayed for an award of custody of the two children of the
marriage. By her answer, the respondent wife denied the
allegation of cruelty and counterclaimed for an award of
custody.

I deal at the outset, in order to dispose of it, with one
particular aspect of this litigation.

The wife made an application under the Family Law Reform Act,
1978 (Ont.), c. 2, seeking a division of family assets. The
divorce proceedings and the application for division of family
assets were heard together. After several Court days a sensible
settlement was made of the claims under the Family Law Reform
Act, 1978. As a result, the Court was left to determine the
reduced set of claims under the Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. D-
8.

Andre Elie Elbaz, the husband, was born on March 19, 1937, so
that he is now 43 years old. He was born in Morocco of orthodox
Jewish parents. His parents moved to Israel in the early
sixties and most of his relatives are now living in Israel or
in France. Although his father has died since, it remains a
close traditional family and he likes to visit them often.

The husband is a man at home in the library. He has a
doctorate of the Sorbonne in French literature. He taught in
Morocco and Nigeria under the auspices of UNESCO. He then
accepted a Fulbright scholarship in the United States. He has
been a professor in French literature at Carleton University
since 1965. To Canada's good fortune, he became a Canadian
citizen in 1970.

Vivian Francoise Elbaz, the wife, was born on July 30, 1947,
so that she is now 33 years old. She was brought up in a Roman
Catholic home. Her parents came to Montreal from France after
World War II and she was born in Canada. Her father, now
retired, was head of the French Department at McGill University
for 20 years. Her brother is a doctor, a specialist in
endocrinology in Montreal. It too is a close-knit family.

The wife also is graced with learning. From McGill she
proceeded to a B.A. with first-class honours in French, modern
Greek and Spanish. From Carleton University, she was graduated
M.A. with distinction in French and Linguistics. She has
completed most of the work courses towards her doctorate. In
March, 1974, she was appointed executive director of the
Canadian Federation for the Humanities which might be described
as the organization acting as the mouthpiece for learned
societies in the humanities and as a liaison with various
Government Departments involved with the humanities.

The husband met his wife in 1967 when he taught summer
courses at McGill and she was still a student. He was then 30;
she was 20. They fell in love and became engaged. The wife
converted to Judaism before their marriage. On July 16, 1969,
they were joined in wedlock by a civil ceremony in Paris. There
followed a religious ceremony of marriage celebrated in Israel
on August 27, 1969.

There are two children of the marriage, a boy and a girl who
were at the time of trial aged respectively ten and six.

Following the marriage, the parties lived in a rented house
in Ottawa. In 1969, they bought their first home which was
known municipally as 1581 Drake Ave. 1971 was a sabbatical year
for the husband. In that year, the parties spent four months in
Israel, two months in Morocco and a month in Paris. But the
wife was not quite at ease in the new world to which her
marriage had transported her. Her mind began to question for
the first time the wisdom of the alliance and whether she had
been seduced by her own emotions into a union of incompatible
temperaments. But her introspective questioning did not unduly
burden the marriage at that stage.

In 1974, the wife began to work full time outside the
matrimonial home. She was employed by the Canadian Federation
for the Humanities as Director of Aid to Scholarly
Publications. With the wife's salary added to the husband's
income, their means were such as would permit the purchase of a
larger home. In August of 1975, they purchased their second
home known municipally as 1260 Lampman Cres. It is a large,
attractive bungalow with a fully-finished basement, on a quiet
residential street. There is a big garden with trees so that
the house might be deep in the country. The children each have
spacious comfortable bedrooms. There is a large playroom
downstairs where they can play in winter. Under the terms of
the settlement of the family assets, the husband purchased the
wife's interest in the former matrimonial home at 1260 Lampman
Cres. so that he is now the sole owner.

As already indicated, the wife had a responsible and
remunerative position which was burdened with an obligation to
travel on a four-day trip at least once a year to attend
learned society conferences. The scope of the husband's
scholarly activities, it should be added, took him outside of
Canada several weeks annually. It so happened that, commencing
in June, 1977, it was necessary for the wife to travel more
frequently. Indeed there was a significant increase in the
frequency and duration of her trips. This led to quarrels which
broke out recurrently during the remainder of their
cohabitation. The husband makes a considerable grievance of his
wife's travelling. He alleges that the increased travelling was
welcome to the wife and that, had she been more considerate of
her family, she would have travelled much less.

That the husband should become restive, I can understand.
Having weighed the evidence, however, I am, on the whole,
satisfied that the increased travelling was necessary to the
discharge of the duties assigned the wife. No doubt a
subsequent promotion was the fruit of never refusing to do what
she was requested to do, and from her salary she made
substantial contributions to the family expenses.

The husband says the marriage was relatively trouble-free
until the disputes which arose about the wife's business trips.
The wife paints a different picture. She asserts that for
several years the strains and stresses of married life had
increased. She levels these complaints against her husband. Her
employment had opened the door to new friends to whom her
husband showed a coolness. His preoccupation with money,
according to the wife, led him to constantly criticize her
handling of household expenses and created much ill-feeling
between them. The husband says that this criticism is unjust.

Naturally I studied the demeanour and personality of the
principal witnesses. In weighing their evidence, an allowance
must be made for a partisanship not always conscious. The
impression they created may be shortly stated. The husband
strikes me as a man of character, not over-addicted to social
life, perhaps holding aloof from his wife's friends and
choosing rather to read in his study. Sincere though he is, he
is sometimes a little too rigid. This rigidity, I think, led
him into a disregard of the deteriorating state of his marriage
until the crisis was on him.

I turn to the wife. In the marriage she no doubt interposed
her own individuality. I see her as pleasant, unpretentious and
easy in all company. For her success as an executive, she is
indebted to her own high intellectual qualities. I should
suppose, however, that in the marital duels she has shown no
undue meekness; she has spice and temperament.

The husband and wife have two things in common: a taste for
intellectual activities and a deep devotion to their children.
Both must share the blame for such failure of the marriage as
was avoidable.

1978 ushered in a cruel year which was destined to rip the
marriage apart. Early in that year, the husband reminded his
wife of his sabbatical leave which was to start on the first of
July and to last for a year. Discussion thereupon took place
between them as to the family accompanying him to Israel for
the sabbatical year. Arrangements were made to that end. The
wife requested, and was granted, leave of absence so that she
could travel with her husband.

But other influences were at work on the wife. The love she
had once felt had fallen into the cracks of the marriage and
vanished. She continued to live with her husband, but began to
have serious reservations about the marriage.

It was in these circumstances that the wife found herself
pregnant in April of 1978. And it was in these circumstances
that she came to a grave decision. She decided upon an
abortion.

That she should have done so is one of the great misfortunes
of the marriage. She has since deeply regretted it. For this
error of judgment an explanation is given which does not
include an excuse. In effect, she says: she was impaled on the
horns of a dreadful dilemma. She did not want to bring a child
into a home of inextinguishable frictions. And, out of the
perplexities of conscience in which duties of conception and
perception conflict with each other, emerged a decision now
beyond recall.

I pause there to point out that the power is not committed to
the Court to determine the moral and social question of
abortion.

There is some conflict in the testimony as to what then
transpired. The husband testified that his wife's discovery of
her pregnancy had been marked by the delight of both of them.
According to him there was not the slightest inkling of a
possible abortion. The first he knew of it was on July 15,
1978, when the abortion was an accomplished fact. The wife
testified to the contrary. On July 5, 1978, she notified her
husband, she says, that she wanted neither to accompany him on
the sabbatical nor to live with him and that she could not
contemplate bringing another child into the home.

I must choose between these two versions. A divided household
promotes a partisanship not always conscious and it is
difficult to get unbiased evidence. I think that the wife did
ventilate her unhappiness in the marriage but I doubt that she
disclosed the contemplated abortion. I have no thought to hold
that the wife was deliberately misleading the Court. I incline
to the view that her recollection of the sequence of events has
been deflected by the passage of time and long-drawn emotional
stress.

Certain it is that the husband did not consent to an
abortion, and the wife makes no pretence that her husband was
privy to the arrangements for the termination of the pregnancy.
To that medical intervention he was a stranger. The
arrangements had all the aspects of subterfuge. On July 10,
1978, the wife informed her husband that she was going to
Montreal for two days in order to reflect upon their marital
problems. On July 15, 1978, her brother telephoned the husband
and informed him that the respondent had gone away with a
friend for the week-end. In truth, she was in New York where
she had secured an abortion.

On the following day -- July 16th, the wife returned home and
laid bare the fact of the abortion. It was for the husband a
traumatic moment. To him, it was an insult to the spiritual
conception of marriage. There was a stormy scene but they
continued to live under the same roof though the wife withdrew
from the matrimonial bedroom.

There was an attempt to effect a full-scale reconciliation.
To that end, the wife took counselling but nothing came of it.
However, they continued to take their meals together as a
family and outwardly there was some semblance of a normal
husband-and-wife relationship. But there were many quarrels
between them and an increasing number of quarrels as time went
on. How was it that these quarrels came to start and who was
the one responsible? Again, there is much discrepancy between
their accounts.

The husband asserts that his wife absented herself from the
home with increasing frequency and without explanation so that
he was alone with the children a great deal of the time. He
states that in the period from January 1, 1978 to October 3,
1978, she was absent out of Ottawa 19 times for a total of 55
nights; that she never told him where he could contact her;
that from early August onward, she became very abusive and
refused to eat with him and the children, and that it was
largely these things that gave rise to their quarrels.

The wife as confidently asserts that her husband had become
increasingly inflexible and critical of her; that he was
opposed to the presence of her friends in the home; that he
made disparaging remarks about her in the presence of the
children, and that his harassment of her made their living
together impossible. The wife gave an accounting of her
absences. It is not my intention to encumber this judgment with
the details of that accounting. I propose to state my
conclusion on this point quite shortly.

I find that the wife's absences from the home were dictated
by the demands of her professional duties. No doubt there were
occasions, not many, when the prospect of a return to an
unhappy home caused her to delay slightly the return. This
begat more friction between husband and wife. In my view,
however, neither was without fault in this deteriorating
situation.

I accept the wife's evidence that prior to each commitment
outside of Ottawa, she would wash the children's clothing,
clean the house and make sure that things were available for
the family when she was away. This arrangement worked tolerably
well except perhaps for the more extended trips. As already
stated, I find that her travel commitments did not have their
origin in a wanton disregard of her motherly duties. As her
travel commitments increased, so did the husband's share of
caring for the children and the home increase. I am bound to
notice that he performed these duties in a praiseworthy manner.

The husband suggests that other circumstances, which came to
his attention later, permit the conclusion that the pregnancy
was terminated with the thought of promoting the wife's
candidacy for a promotion that had unexpectedly presented
itself. I have examined the evidence. To that suggestion, I
cannot yield assent. I find that there was no nexus of relation
between the incident of abortion and the expectation of
promotion.

Despite their quarrels, hope deluded the husband into
thinking that his wife might accompany him to Israel on his
sabbatical leave. But hope was chilled; the wife reaffirmed her
refusal to accompany him there. That meant the husband had to
act quickly to enrol the children for the new year at Hillel
Academy from which they had been withdrawn in expectation of
the sabbatical stay outside of Canada. In this he was
successful. But he accuses his wife of refusing to assist him
with the enrolment. The accounts given of what happened are
contradictory. According to the wife, she at once offered to
take the matter in hand but he excluded her. On this point, I
accept the wife's account as a more natural explanation of the
facts. I note that she paid one-half of the children's tuition
fees.

In October of 1978, the final break occurred between the
parties. By this time they were communicating with each other
only through their respective solicitors. On October 27, 1978,
the husband issued his petition for divorce. For a fugitive
moment peace settled upon them. Pursuant to a consent order of
the Local Master at Ottawa, dated November 17, 1978, the
husband was awarded interim custody of the children and the
wife was granted liberal access.

Like many a decision, the Master's order settled a legal
point without settling the differences between the parties.
That order was succeeded by six motions during the period from
May to September of 1979, touching upon the matter of interim
access. I do not think it necessary to dwell upon these motions
and the resultant orders, though I have read them all, often
more than once. They make it clear that the parties were
tenacious litigants.

The issues between the parties cannot be resolved without due
consideration of the doctrines of their religion. Of this
matter I speak with diffidence and the utmost respect. As
already mentioned, husband and wife are adherents to the Jewish
faith. He was born of orthodox Jewish parents; she converted to
Judaism shortly before their marriage.

Informative evidence of the doctrine of Judaism was given to
the Court. It is appropriate to summarize that evidence
briefly.

There are different communities professing Judaic doctrine.
For example; there are orthodox congregations, and conservative
and reform congregations. It is usually the difference in
degree of observance of the Jewish way of life that sets those
congregations apart. Those who espouse orthodoxy are committed
strictly to the precepts that are recommended by Judaism, of
which the three highest in terms of an orthodox upbringing are:
observance of the Shabbat, the observance of High Holidays and
the keeping of kosher, that is, the dietary regulations.
According to Rabbi Bulka, theologically the highest of the High
Holidays is Shabbat though the Judaic community would probably
perceive it to be Yom Kippur. The Shabbat begins on sundown
Friday and continues until after sunset on Saturday. For a
strictly orthodox family, it would be a totally spiritual day,
a day spent in prayer and contemplation. Going to synagogue on
Shabbat is of special significance because it is the occasion
of an unique prayer service. Apart from the not eating of non-
kosher food, on the Shabbat, there are specific Shabbat
foods. Before the meal there is invocation of blessedness upon
the family. Consistency of observance of Shabbat is one of the
most important aspects of an orthodox upbringing. Not
surprisingly, the matter of the abortion has figured
prominently in the presentation of the case. The classical
Jewish position with respect to abortion is stated in the
testimony of Rabbi Bulka. It is to this effect: only when the
continued existence of the fetus within the mother's womb is
life threatening is there a right to an abortion. Failing that,
abortion is considered equivalent to non-prosecutable murder.
That an abortion in that category might have a substantial
emotional impact on a husband of orthodox religious sensitivity
goes without saying. One, however, must examine the particular
case.

With that background I now come to the allegation of mental
cruelty of such a kind as to render the continued cohabitation
of the spouses intolerable. Particulars to support that
allegation are set out in detail in the petition for divorce. I
have considered them and their cumulative effect on the husband
in arriving at my judgment. The crucial allegations are:

(1) That the wife, without the consent of her husband, caused
an abortion to be performed on herself;

(2) That the wife absented herself from the matrimonial home on
numerous occasions without just cause;

(3) That the wife allowed her husband to take a year's
sabbatical and then changed her mind which caused great
economic and emotional hardship to the husband, and

(4) That the wife unilaterally deserted the conjugal bed.

In Knoll v. Knoll,
1970 CanLII 469 (ON CA)
, [1970] 2 O.R. 169, 10 D.L.R. (3d) 199, 1
R.F.L. 141, Schroeder, J.A., in delivering the judgment of the
Court said at p. 176 O.R., p. 206 D.L.R., p. 149 R.F.L.:

If in the marriage relationship one spouse by his conduct
causes wanton, malicious or unnecessary infliction of pain or
suffering upon the body, the feelings or emotions of the
other, his conduct may well constitute cruelty which will
entitle a petitioner to dissolution of the marriage if in the
Court's opinion, it amounts to physical or mental cruelty "of
such a kind as to render intolerable the continued
cohabitation of the spouses". That is the standard which the
Courts are to apply ...

At p. 179 O.R., p. 209 D.L.R., p. 152 R.F.L., Mr. Justice
Schroeder quotes with approval the case of Lauder v. Lauder,
[1949] P. 277 [at p. 308], Pearce, J.:

"Cruelty cases, more than any other class of case, depend
particularly on a careful estimate of the witnesses. For in a
cruelty case the question is whether this conduct by this man
to this woman or vice versa is cruelty. How far a spouse has
to depart from the normal standards of kindness and self-
control that are the basis of married life and how great
an effect that departure has to have on the other spouse
before it constitutes cruelty is always a question of degree,
depending largely on the temperament, circumstances and
health of each party."

It is the cumulative effects of the acts of the respondent
which must be considered. It is a subjective test. Was this
conduct by this woman to this man cruelty?

It is convenient that I recapitulate in a few sentences what
in my judgment actually happened. The wife took up employment
outside the home with the encouragement of her husband. She
enjoyed her professional duties. As her employment developed,
it absorbed more of her time. That meant that her husband had
to shoulder more of the household tasks and parental duties
than before. He was not disposed to accept that. I think, too,
that there was some professional competitiveness between them.
The husband began to regard the wife's employment travel as
having the effect of depriving the children of the motherly
care to which they were entitled. The husband's view was, in my
judgment, that his wife should conform to his standards. Each
had some of the failings of the other. Both were stubborn.
Incompatibility of temperament led to quarrelling. Neither can
be absolved from blame and want of consideration at times for
the other. It seems to me that much depended on the
personalities of the two parties. I think it probable that the
husband was unconscious of the disastrous extent to which his
rigidity was undermining the marriage. By July of 1978, the
wife was despairing of the marriage. The husband wished to
maintain it. As already stated, I acquit the wife of the charge
of dereliction of her motherly duties. Relations between the
parties broke down and, although they continued to live
together, they did so inharmoniously. Husband and wife
continued to share the household duties. Unhappily the
relations between them did not improve and, in October of 1978,
they separated.

The matter of the abortion is at the forefront of the
husband's case. The abortion without the consent or knowledge
of the husband was far from a trivial act. In my judgment, it
was an act of a weighty nature. No doubt it had some emotional
impact on the husband, but I do not think that it had a really
significant effect on his physical or mental health. And I am
not persuaded that the matter of the abortion, standing alone
or considered in conjunction with all the other circumstances
of the case, rendered intolerable his continued cohabitation.

In the circumstances of this case and with due regard to the
character and physical and mental condition of the parties as I
know it, I have come to the conclusion that the wife's conduct
did not amount to cruelty within the meaning of s. 3(d) of the
Divorce Act.

I do not disguise the fact that I part from the case with
mixed feelings. I am satisfied that there is no reasonable
prospect of reconciliation between the husband and the wife.
The circumstance strongly favours this marriage being
terminated. But the evidence does not establish, in my
judgment, grounds for the granting of a decree nisi.

There remains one very important issue, namely, the custody
of the children of the marriage.

It is familiar law, but it bears repeating, that custody is
viewed not with the idea of adjudicating rights in children but
rather with the idea of making the best disposition possible
for the welfare of the children. That is the pre-eminent
consideration to which the personal considerations of the
parents must yield.

On October 28, 1978, the Local Master at Ottawa, as we have
seen, made an order on consent awarding interim custody to the
husband and granting liberal access to the wife. The children
have been in the care and custody of the father since.
Moreover, the husband has purchased the former matrimonial home
which the children have known as home since 1974. As a parent
the father has been quite excellent. The children are happy and
healthy in their present surroundings. They are doing well at
school. As between the husband and the wife, the dictates of
employment favour the husband with respect to the amount of
time available for personal attention to the children. I
propose to commit the care and custody of these children to the
husband. I can see no advantage to them by awarding custody to
the mother. I take the view that it is best for them at present
to live with their father.

The wife has laudable maternal instincts towards her
children. I find nothing in her conduct as a mother which calls
for censure. She has a good relationship with her children. She
is loving and understanding. Her salary compares favourably
with that of her husband. The wife's proposal involves the
children coming to live with her in a comfortable apartment.
They would continue to attend Hillel Academy.

To quote Ormrod, L.J., in Re K (Minors),
[1977] 2 W.L.R. 33
at p. 42
:

For my part, I do not think that justice between parents in
these cases is ever simple. On the contrary it is a highly
complex question which can very rarely be answered
satisfactorily, and then only after exhaustive investigation.

Until the marriage breakdown, the husband was always with the
children when the wife was absent from the home because of work
commitments. Now she would have to bring in somebody as a
substitute mother during these periods of travel. As I have
already indicated, the father can organize his hours of work so
that there would be relatively little interference with his
day-to-day personal care of the children. They will have the
advantage of continuity if they remain with their father. In my
view, their total welfare would be best served by awarding
custody to the husband.

No one suggests that the wife should be denied access. I
think it should be liberal access including overnight access.
But a particular circumstance makes it difficult to draft a
workable order of access. The difficulty arises in this way.
The children have been raised by the parties in the orthodox
Jewish way of life. In my judgment, it is in their best
interests that they continue to have that upbringing. It is
convenient that access be exercised on the week-ends. Moreover,
a grant of access at any other time would be meaningless
because of the wife's work commitments. The Shabbat begins on
sundown Friday and continues until after sunset on Saturday.
Although the wife is a member of the Jewish faith, she is not
committed totally to every aspect of the orthodox way of life.
The husband, who holds his orthodox beliefs very strongly, not
only wants to live according to his faith but wants his
children to live their lives in the same spirit. He complains
that his wife has participated in activities with the children
in violation of the proper observance of Shabbat. As an example
of the criticism, I cite the charge that, in company of the
children, she went shopping for them on the Shabbat. That
probably happened on a few occasions.

I appreciate and respect the religious convictions of the
husband. Some guidance to the correct approach to this most
difficult question is given in the short judgment of Sir John
Pennycuick in Re K (Minors), supra, at p. 43:

A judge, when deciding what is best for the welfare of a
child, must take into account all the particular
circumstances relevant to that child. I do not doubt that
these circumstances may include the religious and ethical
views prevailing in the environment in which the family
moves, in so far as these affect the child. This may indeed
be a significant factor, but it can never be more than a
factor, in reaching the decision; and in the end the judge
has that single decision to make, namely: What is best for
the welfare of the child?

The wife proposes, inter alia, to take the children on some
week-ends to visit their maternal grandparents in Montreal. I
mention this only for the purpose of illustrating the husband's
fear that it might be hurtful to the children spiritually to be
deprived of the fulfilment of the Shabbat and in lieu thereof
to be exposed to activities which are the antithesis of the
Shabbat.

I appreciate the husband's anxiety. It is certainly a factor
to be taken into account in considering the welfare of the
children. However, I find no evidence that the children have
been adversely affected by the wife not adhering to religious
tradition to the same degree as the husband. In this connection
I note the testimony of Dr. Arthur Leonoff, a clinical
psychologist, that "children generally are able to cope well
with parents having different values so long as the parents
respect each other and the children do not through loyalty
conflicts end up in the middle of something that becomes quite
splitting for them". In my view, a little goodwill and mature
behaviour on the part of the parents can usually make an access
order work.

The wife has stated that she does not feel comfortable in her
husband's synagogue. It strikes me that it would be in the
interests of these two children for the husband to arrange for
their attendance at synagogue subject to the periods when they
are on vacation or in the company of their mother as
hereinafter set out. Because there have been upsets over
access, I intend to specify as best I can the periods of access
in order to avert chronic litigation. Therefore, I would order
that the wife be granted access to the two children as follows:

(1) For the first three week-ends each month from Saturday 1:00
p.m. to Monday 8:00 p.m.; two weeknights each month from 4:00
p.m. to 8:00 p.m., namely, on Wednesday of the week before and
the Wednesday after the week-end when the children are in the
care of the husband, except when the Jewish High Holidays, Rosh
Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Succoth, Passover and Shavuot fall on
such days, then on such days the husband shall have the care of
the children but an equivalent period of time in each case
shall be given to the wife in civic holidays.

(2) For three consecutive days during the mid-winter school
break at Christmas, alternating in succeeding years between the
period from December 25th at 11:00 a.m. to December 27th at
8:00 p.m. inclusive and the period from December 31st at 11:00
a.m. to January 2nd at 8:00 p.m. inclusive. In the event a
Jewish High Holiday should fall on such a day, then an
equivalent period of time shall be made up to the wife in civic
holidays or in the long school vacation period of July and
August.

(3) Neither parent shall remove either child from Canada
without an order of this Court or without the consent in
writing of both parties.

(4) In the event either child requires medical treatment, both
parents shall be consulted and participate in any decision
relating to the medical treatment.

(5) Each parent shall have the right to receive information
relating to the children from the school administration and
teachers of the school or schools which the children attend.

(6) The wife, whenever the children are in her care, shall
ensure that the children eat kosher food and observe as far as
reasonably possible the Shabbat, subject to the right to travel
with the children on Shabbat with tickets purchased in advance.
I use the words "as far as reasonably possible" bearing in mind
unusual situations. To illustrate: last summer the wife took
the children on a vacation to Prince Edward Island. It
happened, as I am advised, that there was no synagogue there.
To the orthodox, the history of the Jewish people is not
because they contemplate God from an intellectual point of view
but because of observance. The wife should therefore avoid
exposing the children to influences that are in conflict with
orthodox Jewish spiritual values.

It remains for me to consider the proper amount for support
of these two children. No evidence of the cost of support was
given. Both parents seem anxious, however, that the children
have an education and a standard of living commensurate with
their parents' stations in life. The husband's salary is about
$30,000 a year; the wife's about $32,000. Neither has
substantial assets. At one time, I indicated that I thought
$175 per month per child and one-half of the fees at Hillel
Academy might be a proper award. On further reflection and
having regard to other benefits conferred on the children by
the wife such as purchases of clothing and payment of
vacations, I have reached the conclusion that an order of $160
per month per child and one-half of their fees at Hillel
Academy would be proper. I am reasonably confident that the
wife will continue to make purchases for their benefit. And she
will have the expense of caring for them during the periods of
liberal access.

It seems to me that this is a case in which the husband and
the wife should each pay his or her own costs. True it is that
the petition for divorce was dismissed but the evidence in that
controversy was so closely bound to the issue of custody and
access that it did not add significantly to the length of the
trial.

I add a concluding observation. I am mindful that I have been
guilty of some degree of repetition in this judgment, but I owe
the appellate Court the duty of providing what assistance I can
if the matter goes before them. Whether a judgment be right or
wrong, it undoubtedly provides some assistance to the Court and
the parties by at least indicating the processes through which
my mind has passed.

Judgment accordingly.
